newsitem.title: UK: Options - LME aluminium slump prompts put demand.
newsitem.headline: Options - LME aluminium slump prompts put demand.

text.p: The slump in aluminium prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) this week prompted fresh demand for put options on nearby months and in 1997, traders said.
Business was generally slow, although volumes tended to pick up after the October options declaration, which passed quietly on Wednesday morning.
"Overall it's been a disappointing week, but we saw more aluminium put buying for November and December," a trader said.
The buying centred on close-to-the-money strikes around $1,375 a tonne at the start of the week moving down to strikes around $1,300 later as prices slumped, another trader added.
Benchmark three month futures fell to a fresh 2-1/4 year low of $1,340 on Thursday, down from a peak of $1,420 last week and a high this week so far of $1,402.
Nearby volatilities moved higher, with November quoted at around 18.75 percent volatility early on Friday from 18.25 percent a week ago.
Producers appeared to be getting nervous about the prolonged period of price weakness, with forward put buying emerging.
"It's the first fresh producer hedging we've seen for some time, and they appear to be getting nervous," said one trader.
"We saw three months/average 1997 move in to $60/64 contango from $70/75, so there was a little forward selling against those options," he added.
The trader said market makers were happy to grant forward aluminium puts, because they were generally long of them while being short of upside calls.

Another trader said forward put buying was at a range of strikes from close-to-the-money to downside, trading at 18.25 to 18.50 percent volatility. The bulk of the business was seen done in the first half of the year.
Dealers also saw some consumer call buying for the second half of 1997, with December $1,650 and $1,700 calls trading at around 18.50 percent.
There was talk 1997 upside calls were as strong as 19 percent early on Friday, reflecting the slight volatility skew towards upside calls.
"I think this was genuine consumer type business on the late 1997 calls," said one trader.
Copper business was slow and mixed, with booksquaring and switching going on for nearby months ahead of next week's annual LME Week shindig in London.
"Copper has been very quiet. People are just squaring themselves up ahead of LME Week, when very few people will be at their desks," said one dealer.
Another saw granting of puts as demand for calls subsided.
November and December volatility was quoted at around 26.50 percent early on Friday, down slightly on the week.
The options declaration passed quietly after the sharp rally a week ago failed to trigger a move above the key $2,000 strike.
In the event October copper was indicated at below $1,900 when options were declared.
Forward copper options trade was said to be slow this week.
Zinc volatilities edged lower nearby, reflecting relatively dull conditions on the underlying futures market.
Dealers noted selling of at-the-money strangles and doubles.
Tin volatilities picked up earlier in the week as prices slumped to 16-month lows on Tuesday. But granting was emerging into the strength, traders said.
November volatility was quoted at around 14 percent early on Friday from 11 percent a week ago.
Lead and nickel options business was slow.
--Mike Collett-White, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8057
